title: How Long to Do a Physiological Sigh: 1 to 3 Sighs or 5 Minutes

copy.cover_headline: Your quick reset: three sighs, about 30 seconds

points.headline: Two doses, two different jobs
points.body: One to three sighs (about 10 to 30 seconds) for a quick reset. About five minutes of cyclic sighing as a daily practice. Only the five-minute version has been tested in a trial.

points.headline: How to do a physiological sigh
points.body: Inhale through your nose for 2 to 3 seconds. Add a small top-up sip, about 1 second. Exhale slowly through your mouth for 6 to 8 seconds. One normal breath, then repeat 2 or 3 times.

points.headline: How to tell you've done enough
points.body: Your exhale lengthens by itself, your jaw unclenches, your shoulders drop. That might take one sigh or three. Stop right away if you feel tingly or lightheaded.

points.headline: What the trial found (and didn't)
points.body: In a 2023 Stanford trial of 108 people over 28 days, cyclic sighing lifted mood more than mindfulness. Anxiety fell about equally. Sleep, HRV and resting heart rate didn't change.

points.headline: Gentle beats more
points.body: Keep the top-up a small sip and let the exhale fall out. Stacking big, fast sighs can tip into over-breathing. A gentle, brief reset is closer to what your body does on its own.

copy.instagram_caption:
The feed has wound you up. Coming back down can take less than a minute.

Here's a 30-second script for mid-scroll: put the phone face-down (no need to put it away), do two or three slow sighs, check your jaw and shoulders, then breathe easily for about 30 seconds. After that, decide whether to pick the phone back up. The feed will be exactly where you left it.

Your body already does this on its own. People sigh spontaneously about every five minutes, and in one lab study those natural sighs were followed by lower muscle tension. A deliberate sigh tries to borrow that reflex, which is why we keep it gentle and few.

If breathing out through your mouth feels odd, nose-only sighing works too. The Stanford protocol allowed it.

Want the daily practice instead? About five minutes of cyclic sighing is the dose that was studied. Our free physiological sigh timer paces it so you don't have to count.

A safety note: do it sitting or standing still, never while driving. If you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, a history of fainting, or find breath focus triggers panic, go gently or check with a clinician first. It isn't a treatment, and for persistent anxiety or sleep trouble, talk to a professional.
